item.description: Bacteria get a bad reputation—with all the outbreaks, infections and deaths. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: The Jackdaw field will start supplying gas to homes and businesses from the end of the month, the government said Here is an explainer by Jill Ambrose about the Jackdaw decision. But environmental groups have condemned the decision. Ami McCarthy, head of politics for Greenpeace UK , said: Approving Jackdaw shows the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy. item.title: Massive study of 460,000 people challenges ultra-processed food cancer fears
item.description: A massive study of more than 460,000 Americans found that ultra-processed foods were not associated with increased colorectal cancer risk overall, challenging a widely held assumption. While processed meat was linked to higher cancer incidence, ultra-processed whole grains and dairy products were associated with lower incidence. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Astronomers uncover the engine behind the most powerful stellar flares in the Kepler field
item.description: A new study led by researchers at the Konkoly Observatory of the HUN-REN Research Centre for Astronomy and Earth Sciences (HUN-REN CSFK) in Budapest has revealed what makes a distant red giant star the most explosively active in the entire Kepler field—and the answer lies in a surprisingly subtle interplay between a close stellar companion, vast dark starspots and a highly efficient internal magnetic dynamo. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australia urged to put biodiversity at the heart of planning as global targets slip out of reach
item.description: The world is falling short of its biodiversity commitments because nature is still treated as an afterthought in decisions about housing, infrastructure, agriculture, energy, mining and conservation, according to a new UNSW report. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Too much RNA can starve cells of energy, scientists discover
item.description: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. A new study found that excess RNA, including the normally essential messenger RNA (mRNA), can directly disrupt mitochondria without relying on the immune system. The discovery could help explain how viral infections and certain aging-related diseases damage cells. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: AI reveals how a warming climate will intensify NZ's most extreme downpours
item.description: The most damaging weather events are the record-breaking "one-in-100-year" disasters communities have usually only seen once. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The ocean's most abundant 'loner' microbe has a sticky second life
item.description: The oxygen in about every other breath we take comes from microscopic cells—phytoplankton—drifting in the surface of the ocean. Among them is Prochlorococcus, the smallest and most abundant photosynthetic organism in the seas. It single-handedly accounts for roughly 10% of all the carbon that the land and the oceans pull from the atmosphere each year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tackling Lake Erie's algal blooms requires targeted conservation strategies
item.description: Anyone living along the coast of Lake Erie will be well aware of the periodic algal blooms that appear on its surface. The greenish blooms can cause rashes and other health problems and pose risks to both humans and animals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
item.description: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Genomes of 20 eastern Finnish species provide unique insights into species' adaptations to local conditions
item.description: In recent years, researchers at the University of Eastern Finland have been both leading and contributing to collaborative genome projects. These efforts have produced reference-quality genome assemblies for the Finnish brown hare and the mountain hare, as well as the Saimaa ringed seal, in collaboration with research partners. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s CASALS Instrument Bridges Gaps in 3D Maps of Earth’s Surface
item.description: From orbit, today’s space-based laser instruments measure Earth’s forests and terrain one narrow line at a time. Between those lines are enormous gaps that include millions of acres of land scientists never directly measure. NASA’s CASALS instrument will blend machine learning with an ultra-compact lidar instrument to adaptively ‘sweep’ large swaths of Earth’s surface. This […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: FOSSA Systems e IENAI Space han puesto en órbita el primer satélite español con propulsión eléctrica
item.description: Este 20 de octubre de 2026 se ha lanzado un satélite 6U desde Cabo Cañaveral, Florida, a bordo de un cohete Falcon 9, de SpaceX. El lanzamiento, que forma parte de la misión compartida Bandwagon-5, ha sido todo un hito español, ya que es el primer satélite de propulsión eléctrica de fabricación española. Más español que la paella . El satélite ha sido fabricado por la compañía española Fossa Systems . Es el número 27 que se lanza desde 2020; por lo que, según comunicados recogidos por Actualidad Aeroespacial , sería ya la empresa de España que más objetos ha puesto en órbita. En cuanto a sus… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Parents and nongamers struggle to identify video game loot boxes
item.description: New research has found parents, guardians and nongamers may struggle to recognize video game loot boxes, their defining features and the digital receipts linked to purchases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
item.description: A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Atomic memory keeps distant ions entangled for about 10 seconds
item.description: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices and allow them to exchange information encoded in the quantum states of particles, could enable more secure communications. To build these networks, physicists need to devise strategies that allow distant particles to share quantum states, preserving them long enough to perform calculations or enable communication between devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can surplus-food apps have too much competition?
item.description: Apps that let businesses sell surplus food at a discount in "surplus bags" have become a popular way to keep edible food out of landfills while giving consumers access to lower-cost meals and groceries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells
item.description: Scientists have turned blood cells from an 80-year-old into neural stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20, effectively reversing more than 60 years of cellular aging in the laboratory. The discovery offers a new way to investigate how cells become younger and could help researchers better understand age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Q&A: Do new platform features hurt hiring chances for competitive gig workers?
item.description: Whether they are driven by economic necessity or a desire for greater control over their careers, a growing number of workers are turning to online gig-work platforms to supplement their income with freelance projects like coding or website design. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Synchronized bodily responses do not always reflect cooperation, study finds
item.description: Sometimes, while people are interacting with each other, their movements and physiological responses can fall into step. Some past studies have linked synchronized bodily responses to cooperation and being attuned to the emotions of others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Musk talks up potential merger of SpaceX and Tesla
item.description: As SpaceX reports blockbuster quarterly earnings, CEO Elon Musk floats the possibility of merging the rocketry and AI firm with his electric car company Tesla. Also in this edition: OpenAI reveals more agent misbehaviour as market turmoil hits data centre companies, and France's political crisis exacerbates its bond market rout. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: ‘Jackdaw means we pay our mortgages’: relief in Aberdeen over gasfield approval
item.description: Few believe decision will bring back city’s boom years, but workers hope it will secure North Sea jobs for now UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean? As recently as 2012, Aberdeen boasted the highest concentration of millionaires in the UK. An ATM reportedly had the highest withdrawal rate in Europe in the 90s, as oil and gas wealth flowed through the city. House prices skyrocketed in the scramble for space as fossil fuel firms transformed the city’s grand granite houses into company offices. But that was then. Today, “for sale” and… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Just 4 minutes a day can dramatically improve strength after 65
item.description: A new Penn State study suggests that just four minutes of daily strength training can significantly improve mobility and physical function in older adults. After 12 weeks, participants showed meaningful gains in balance, leg strength, and their ability to stand up from a chair, all important factors for maintaining independence and reducing fall risk. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: South Korea launches new bid to guide crowd-pulling shark to sea
item.description: South Korean authorities began a new attempt Wednesday to coax a shark-turned-viral sensation back to sea, with falling temperatures in the Busan canal where it is stranded raising concerns for its survival. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover just shattered the all-time off-world driving record
item.description: NASA’s Perseverance rover has shattered a historic space exploration record, traveling farther across another world than any vehicle before it. Its advanced self-driving system helped it surpass Opportunity’s 28.06-mile record in just five and a half years, a feat that previously took nearly 15. Now, Perseverance is exploring some of the oldest rocks in the solar system, searching for clues about ancient Martian environments that may once have supported life. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Prized wild pepper at risk in Madagascar's shrinking forests
item.description: A rare wild pepper endemic to Madagascar and prized by international chefs is facing an uncertain future, a victim of its own success and the destruction of its forest habitat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More current with less calcium: Computational models help solve longstanding ion channel evolution mystery
item.description: In the early 1980s, scientists observed an anomaly. Embedded within cell membranes, they identified ion channels with extraordinarily high conductance. These so-called "BK" (Big K, or Big Potassium) channels had roughly 10 times the unitary conductance (i.e., conductance per individual channel molecule) of other potassium channels, enabling much more efficient, rapid transport of potassium ions. And while later structural characterization explained how this happened, no one could understand why. That is, until now. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Transparent minispheres reveal that some look-alike cancer drugs part ways in 3D
item.description: Researchers at Uppsala University have adapted Cell Painting, a widely used imaging method in drug discovery, to look at individual cells inside small 3D clusters of cancer cells. Two drugs that looked almost identical in ordinary flat cell cultures behaved differently in 3D, and the team linked the difference to how each drug switches on the cell's p53 stress response. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A First Nation community in Canada is using a data center to preserve its heritage
item.description: For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data center to help preserve its heritage. Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: SpaceX turns a profit after a string of losses as its satellite and computer leasing businesses soar
item.description: SpaceX reported a bigger quarterly profit than expected Tuesday as its satellite communications operations and its business of leasing computing power to other companies boomed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Targeting a particular gene may improve tea plants' flavor and cold tolerance
item.description: Research in New Phytologist reveals a gene that regulates tea plants' flavor and cold tolerance, providing insights on how to expand the potential for better-tasting tea to be grown in a wider variety of locations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: U.S. antipoverty tax credit expansion may have unintended costs for children's development
item.description: As part of U.S. welfare reforms in the 1990s to provide adequate financial support to low-income families while avoiding disincentivizing work, policymakers expanded the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC). This change encouraged people to work more by giving greater benefits with greater earned income, and single mothers faced stronger incentives to enter the workforce than married mothers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
item.description: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: China builds the world’s smallest wearable brain monitor with a cortex-wide view
item.description: Chinese scientists have developed what they say is the world’s smallest wearable mini brain monitor that can track the activity of thousands of neurons at the same time. Weighing in at one gram (0.35 oz), the wireless “Airscope” is the lightest device of its kind and enables researchers to track a wider range of brain activity in untethered laboratory animals. The device was jointly developed by scientists from Tsinghua University and the Chinese PLA Medical School, and detailed in a paper... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Guatemala gains its first endemic bird in American Ornithological Society's 67th supplement
item.description: The 67th Supplement to the American Ornithological Society's (AOS's) Check-list of North American Birds, which was published today in Ornithology, includes several significant updates to the classification of bird species found in North America, Central America and the Caribbean. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
item.description: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A magnetar can be born when two neutron stars touch
item.description: All neutron stars have intense magnetic fields. The typical magnetic field of a neutron star is about 100,000 times stronger than the strongest magnetic fields we can create on Earth. But about 1% of neutron stars have even stronger magnetic fields. Known as magnetars, their magnetic fields can be 1,000 times stronger than a regular magnetic field. They are a likely cause of powerful transient events such as soft gamma-ray repeaters and fast radio bursts. A new study looks at how magnetars might form. The findings are published on the arXiv preprint server. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Women farmers need better financing to benefit from AI
item.description: Public and private investments must address the financial barriers preventing women from benefiting fully from digital technologies and artificial intelligence as multiple global crises and aid cuts bite. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are partisan politics even changing up our accents? They just might be, y'all
item.description: With the midterms fast approaching, communicating just the right message has been top of mind on all sides of the political aisle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find 10 different diets linked to slower aging
item.description: A study by DZNE finds that healthy eating is associated with slower biological aging—and that there is more than one way to eat healthily. The researchers examined ten dietary patterns considered healthy, including the Mediterranean, Nordic, and a plant-based diet, as well as the DASH diet, which is designed to help lower blood pressure. The findings are published in the journal Nature Communications. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Controlled vapor treatment guides molecules into highly oriented soft quasicrystals
item.description: Molecules can spontaneously organize into complex, ordered structures through a process known as self-assembly. Among these structures, soft quasicrystals display unusual patterns that do not repeat regularly like conventional crystals. However, producing such structures with a uniform orientation over large areas remains a major challenge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Major repairs needed to save Horseshoe Bay Lagoon
item.description: Volunteer researcher Chris Hopper, JCU's adjunct professor Eric Wolanski and independent researcher Natalie K. Dowling examined the impact of saltwater and erosion on Horseshoe Bay Lagoon, a freshwater lagoon and one of the few swamps with bulkuru sedge—also known as water chestnut—on the Magnetic Island (Yunbenun). The study is published in the journal Applied Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rare solar radiation storm gives scientists clearest picture yet of flight risks
item.description: The most comprehensive data set ever collected from Earth's atmosphere during a solar radiation event has highlighted the importance of better-coordinated radiation monitoring for aviation safety, according to new research led by the University of Surrey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shortening Canadian teacher education risks devaluing the profession of teaching
item.description: Recently, shorter teacher certification programs have been introduced in different Canadian provinces. These programs are being implemented in Alberta, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Québec. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Where El Niño may impact California coastal areas this winter
item.description: Driving across Highway 37 in the San Francisco Bay Area on the best of days already feels like driving on top of water. Buffeted on both sides by marshlands hosting egrets, herons, ducks and a handful of endangered species, the sea-level highway is a major connector linking Marin, Sonoma, Napa and Solano counties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers study how AI could improve weed management
item.description: Advances in weed management technology could reduce reliance on herbicides and manual labor, but a new review from the University of Mississippi and Cornell University indicates those tools also bring steep costs and potential challenges. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03355-x The United Nations’ latest climate report is a stark reminder that limiting warming to the safest levels is now likely out of reach. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Shipwrecks can become thriving reefs, but may contain hidden toxic time bombs
item.description: Late last year, scientists in Germany published findings on a World War II munitions dump in the Baltic Sea. Some may dismiss the dump as hazardous waste, but to marine biologists it was something far more exciting: a thriving ecosystem. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Judging faces without personality labels uncovers key patterns in first impressions
item.description: Imagine sitting on a city bus full of strangers. Look around at the people riding with you. If you needed help, how would you choose whom to trust? By scanning people's faces, your brain is already making interpretations about their personalities by judging certain facial features. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
item.description: Investigative genetic genealogy can help hunt down criminals but raises worries over privacy. Fuente: BBC News - Business.

item.title: Mystery skeleton found in Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally have an identity
item.description: The identity of a mysterious skeleton found in a Roman sarcophagus in the grounds of Westminster Abbey more than 150 years ago appears closer to being solved. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Study identifies ‘circadian depression’ as affecting nearly a quarter of more than 11,000 participants Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian researchers have identified a new subtype of depression – termed “circadian depression” – linked to disruptions in the body’s internal clock, which they believe is less responsive to traditional antidepressant treatments. In a study published in British Journal of Psychiatry, involving clinical and genetic data from 11,380 Australians with mostly severe and recurrent depression, researchers identified circadian… Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: Caribbean islands were once the center of diversity for barn owls
item.description: Legend has it that a giant elfin, owl-like creature called the chickcharney haunts the islands of the Bahamas. Those who encounter this cryptid on cordial terms are said to be blessed with good luck. Those who disrespect the chickcharney, however, don't fare as well. "If you see one shoe in the field, it means that chickcharney came, picked up this person and took them away," said Jessica Oswald, recounting a story she was told in the Bahamas. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Northern Australia is a 'lifeboat' for critically endangered green sawfish
item.description: Green sawfish, distinguished by their long, sharklike bodies and tooth-lined "saw" on the front of their heads, are on the verge of extinction, largely due to overfishing and habitat loss. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Christina Koch, astronauta del Artemis II: “La gente se preocupa por si cambiaremos la Luna igual que hemos cambiado la Tierra; esa es nuestra elección”
item.description: Tras completar con éxito el histórico sobrevuelo lunar, se conoció una frase que la astronauta de la NASA pronunció mientras realizaba la misión Artemis II Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Male seahorse pouch proteins may help remove toxic waste from developing embryos
item.description: Male seahorses, fishes that belong to the Syngnathidae family, show a distinctive reproductive strategy in which males carry developing embryos in a brood pouch. Their most distinctive feature is the brood pouch on the ventral side of the male fish, into which the female fish transfers her eggs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Diverse and sustained social activities may boost cognition in older age
item.description: Diverse and sustained social activities may boost cognitive performance and slow the decline in brain health associated with aging, suggest the findings of a large international study, published online in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Soybean waste yields 3D-printable material that could help repair skin
item.description: Transforming a soybean processing byproduct into a material for skin protection and repair is the prospect outlined by a study that used okara, a residue from the production of tofu and soy-based beverages, to obtain a bioactive, biodegradable, 3D-printable biomaterial. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are transgender sports bans really about protecting women? Survey data tells a different story
item.description: Relatively few transgender athletes participate in high school and collegiate sports. Still, since 2020, 27 states have passed laws banning them from participating in sports based on their gender identity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A hidden rivalry between two quantum states at the heart of superconductors
item.description: Transmitting electricity without losing any energy may sound impossible, yet this is precisely the promise of superconductivity. For nearly 40 years, scientists have been working to understand materials that exhibit this remarkable property at relatively high temperatures. Unlocking their secrets could one day help make power grids more efficient, enhance medical technologies and support the development of quantum computing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Feral—and threatened? Endangered camels, banteng and hog deer have found an unexpected refuge in Australia
item.description: Millions of large feral animals roam Australia. Pigs, camels, deer, horses, water buffalo, cattle and goats were introduced deliberately as transport, livestock or to hunt. Many have since established wild populations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How buying weapons can harm a country's economy
item.description: Some wars are predictable. There are conflicts past and present which have been more or less expected because of economic and social conditions, a country's history or that of its neighbors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Machine learning reveals potential warning signal for polar vortex disruptions
item.description: The polar vortex, a swirling mass of cold air encircling the North Pole, is sometimes disrupted by sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) events, unleashing waves of frigid air that penetrate farther south than usual. Temperatures across North America and Europe drop precipitously when this happens, but such events remain hard to predict, meaning we can't easily warn people when SSW is imminent. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Terror of kings': Why the 1066 appearance of Halley's Comet terrified the medieval world
item.description: A sequence on the Bayeux Tapestry shows King Harold alongside a crowd gazing at the sky, beneath the embroidered caption Isti mirant stella ("those people marvel at the star"). Above Harold sits Halley's Comet, with ghostlike invasion boats in the border below—a Norman framing of Harold as a doomed usurper whose betrayal invited destruction. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New study reveals the high financial value of privacy in legal proceedings
item.description: A new Management Science study provides rare real-world evidence that people are willing to give up thousands of dollars to prevent sensitive information about their health and income from becoming public. The research, developed over five years by an international team, has now also laid the foundation for a European research project led by Ehud Guttel of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Oxygen collisions show evidence of jet quenching, a signature of early-universe matter
item.description: New results from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) provide strong evidence that smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light generates a quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a type of matter that existed just after the birth of the universe. The data, just published in Physical Review Letters, show that energetic jets of particles lose energy as they traverse the hot, dense matter left in the collision's wake. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tofu is the winner. Scientist creates new holistic scoring system to measure the impact of food
item.description: Consumers are increasingly confronted with conflicting information surrounding how much protein they should have and which protein sources are healthiest, most sustainable, and best value for money. Cambridge research has uncovered the truth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Using eyedrops in space—wearable patch offers a new approach
item.description: Applying eyedrops is difficult in space, where there is almost no gravity. A KAIST research team has developed a wearable patch that delivers eyedrops to the eye without relying on gravity. The research team was led by Professor Ki-Hun Jeong from the Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, in collaboration with a research team led by Professor Se Joon Woo from Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. The paper is published in the journal Sensors and Actuators B: Chemical. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From seafloor depths to fishing activity, free software brings ocean data together
item.description: For scientists studying the ocean, finding the right data can sometimes be as challenging as figuring out what to do with it. Want to know seafloor depth, the location of underwater mountains or sea surface temperatures? The information exists, but it can take considerable time and computer coding to pull it together from different sources and get it into the proper format. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why is it so hard to spot a liar? Expert explains the psychology of deception
item.description: From The Traitors to everyday life, we often mistake nervousness, confidence or group suspicion for signs of deception. Dr Nadja Heym, Associate Professor in Personality Psychology and Psychopathology, explains why spotting a liar is harder than we think. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland
item.description: Editor’s Note: This article was originally published on Oct. 15, 2026, and has been updated to correct the location of the flights. A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from […] Fuente: NASA.

item.description: Democratic backsliding can be tricky to spot. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supercomputer reveals how size could shape the future of nanomedicine
item.description: Scientists have long been interested in cellular nanodiscs, tiny particles made from natural cell membranes that mimic many of the functions of living cells. While previous studies demonstrated the therapeutic potential of nanodiscs for drug delivery, detoxification and vaccines, one fundamental question remained unanswered: How does size influence how well they work? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Water as we've never known it: Physicists test water beyond Earth-like conditions
item.description: Water isn't always as it seems. Under extreme conditions, such as those found on other planets, it has been discovered to change its atomic structure, giving it the means to alter its appearance and other properties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Despega con éxito misión que explorará una de las lunas de Marte por primera vez en la historia
item.description: Despegó con éxito el cohete que lleva la primera sonda que explorará Fobos, la mayor de las lunas de Marte. El vehículo espacial no tripulado Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) llegará en agosto de 2027 al astro marciano y volverá nen 2031 con las primeras muestras del sistema del planeta rojo, lo que permitiría a los científicos conocer más información sobre el origen de nuestro Sistema Solar entre otros datos. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: Aurora supercomputer powers two of the largest cosmological simulations to date
item.description: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory have completed two of the largest cosmological simulations ever performed. Each simulation modeled the evolution of 13.4 trillion dark matter particles across a region 28.6 billion light-years wide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Smoking gun' may help solve mystery of high-temperature superconductivity
item.description: Superconductivity has many important practical applications, including creating powerful magnets used in high-resolution medical scans, transporting electricity efficiently and building ultrasensitive measuring devices. Until now, understanding exactly what lay behind this unique phenomenon at high temperatures has eluded scientists over many decades. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fluorescent reaction maps reveal how catalyst activity changes with operating conditions
item.description: Catalysts spur chemical reactions used across industries, from producing fuels and medicines to manufacturing chemicals and treating pollutants. Improving their performance requires understanding where and how reactions happen on their surfaces. However, conventional measurements average the activity of many catalyst particles, concealing local differences that could hold clues to designing more effective materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a cold pulse in the Northwest Atlantic reshaped East Coast fisheries
item.description: Fishers in the Northeast began noticing an unusual shift in the summer of 2023. Some familiar catches, including shortfin and longfin squid, declined, while cold-water species such as mackerel bounced back from years of decline. A new study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans finds that a pulse of cold, fresh water brought unusually cold conditions to the region, disrupting fisheries from New England to the Mid-Atlantic. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The bioeconomy is gaining ground worldwide, report shows
item.description: Oil and natural gas still account for the vast majority of the world's energy and raw materials, with all the associated environmental and biodiversity consequences. The bioeconomy is an approach to overcoming this dependence: Instead of using fossil fuels, it uses renewable resources such as plants, microorganisms and organic waste. The goal is for economic growth to go hand in hand with protecting species, the climate and soils. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wall Street researchers just used Claude to design a drug. The experiment has spawned a new investment thesis.
item.description: For years, artificial-intelligence evangelists have boasted about the technology’s capacity to revolutionize drug development and medical research. Fuente: MarketWatch.

item.title: Filling the gaps in global rainfall maps
item.description: Global rainfall maps are built from observations collected by multiple satellites, but they have an important limitation. The satellites that provide these measurements cannot see the whole Earth at once. As a result, some regions of these maps can have no valid observations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Leptospirosis is a neglected zoonotic disease caused by pathogenic Leptospira bacteria and can affect humans and animals, including horses. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Custom frame timing captures ultrafast events across five orders of magnitude in time
item.description: Most conventional methods of ultrafast photography use evenly spaced intervals in which images are taken, but new developments have shown how much can be left out of the story, especially when multiple timescales are involved. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Seven-minute virtual reality intervention helps students tackle stress and exam anxiety
item.description: A seven-minute virtual reality (VR) intervention can help students feel calmer, less anxious and better able to cope with academic pressure, according to new research from City St George's. The findings, published in Scientific Reports, come at a time when schools and universities across the U.K. seek new approaches to support student well-being amid growing concerns about stress, anxiety and overwhelm among young people. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook. item.title: A century of records paints a worrying picture for Europe's bees
item.description: In most parts of Europe, bees have become less widespread during the last 100 years, according to a new study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Research concludes that Shakespeare wrote 'Edward III' with Marlowe
item.description: Dr. Rory Loughnane, a reader in early modern studies in the School of Humanities, has confirmed "beyond any reasonable doubt" that William Shakespeare was the principal writer of "Edward III" and that it was written in collaboration with his so-called rival and Canterbury's most famous poet and playwright, Christopher Marlowe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Limited waste collection services in rural communities linked to high microplastic levels in Mekong River
item.description: Plastics are accumulating in ecosystems around the world, and their tiny fragments can collect and carry chemical pollutants and pathogens into plants, animals and people. When fishermen in Cambodia's Mekong River became alarmed about the amounts of plastic they were hauling up with each catch, they reached out to scientists for help. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI challenges math by solving the unsolvable
item.description: Announcements over recent months that artificial intelligence models have cracked previously unsolvable problems are shaking top-level mathematicians to the core, and they are now asking themselves: Where do we come in? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unraveling DNA repair: How cells protect their genetic blueprint
item.description: Every cell in the human body faces a chronic challenge: protecting its DNA. Whenever cells divide, their genetic material must be copied accurately. But DNA is continuously under attack, and when damage goes unrepaired, it can threaten genome stability and contribute to the progression of disease. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Christina Koch, astronauta del Artemis II: “No hay nada que te prepare para ver a tu planeta iluminado como si fuera de día”

item.title: How the aftermath of negotiations turns 'winners' into 'losers,' and vice versa
item.description: At its best, negotiation is the art of mutual value creation. But once created, that value must be capitalized upon in the post-negotiation environment. That means the formal end of negotiations is often only the end of the beginning. Time will tell whether the gains and losses sustained during a negotiation are as solid as they seem when the counterparties get up from the table. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cost-analysis tool allows coastal communities to see and estimate benefits of investing in storm-protection measures
item.description: Today, as part of the official release of California's Fifth Climate Change Assessment, researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, have launched a platform, data and tools that community leaders can use to estimate the block-by-block climate risks and the cost-effectiveness of adaptation solutions for reducing coastal damages. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Orionid meteor shower is coming. Here's how and when to watch
item.description: The Orionids—one of two major meteor showers caused by remnants from Halley's Comet—will peak this week, though a large moon will dim visibility until after it sets late at night. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Jackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentials What does the approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean? The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs. Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. item.title: PermitAI team delivers a one-stop shop for federal permitting data
item.description: The PermitAI team at the Department of Energy's Pacific Northwest National Laboratory has changed how federal agencies search past environmental permitting decisions. Now it is taking that access one step further with two newly released publicly available resources that give instant access to both past decisions and live government data. Together, they cover the full federal permitting life cycle. Fuente: Phys.org.
